s: Nexstar Media Group DEF 14A filed 30 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership table as of 20 Apr 2026: 1,862,765 shares, 6.1 percent
m: 1,862,765 shares (975,956 held by PS Sook Ltd, 886,809 direct) times the 186.14 dollar NXST close of 21 Aug 2026 = 347 million dollars
did: Founded Nexstar in 1996 by buying one money-losing station, WYOU in Wilkes-Barre, and rolled up roughly 200 more, taking Media General in 2017 for 4.6 billion dollars, Tribune Media in 2019 for 6.4 billion and TEGNA in 2025, plus The CW network and NewsNation.
why: Retransmission consent. The 1992 Cable Act let broadcasters charge cable and satellite carriers for their signal, and Sook was among the first to demand cash rather than channel space. Scale multiplied that leverage, and sidecar shared-services deals let him exceed the FCC ownership cap market by market.
obst: In 2005 he pulled Nexstar signals off Cox Cable in three markets for months rather than give the signal away free, taking a ratings and revenue hit that his own board questioned, to establish that broadcasters would be paid cash for retransmission.
turn: The 2019 Tribune Media acquisition, which made Nexstar the largest US station owner by household reach and forced the FCC ownership-cap fight into the open.

s: Matador Resources DEF 14A filed 29 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership as of 13 Apr 2026: 5,450,980 shares, 4.4 percent
m: 5,450,980 shares (Sage Resources LP, family non-GST trusts and GRATs for which he holds power of substitution) times the 58.38 dollar MTDR close of 21 Aug 2026 = 318 million dollars
did: Started Foran Oil in 1983 with 270,000 dollars from 17 friends and neighbours, folded it into Matador Petroleum in 1988 and sold that to Tom Brown Inc in 2003; the following Monday he founded Matador Resources, IPO'd it in 2012 and built it into a top-20 US producer centred on the Delaware Basin.
why: He bought Delaware Basin acreage in Loving and Lea counties from 2011, before the play was de-risked and while everyone else was chasing the Midland side, then built San Mateo Midstream with Five Point so Matador collected the gathering, processing and produced-water margin that peers paid away to third parties.
obst: Matador was rebuilt as a Haynesville gas company; the 2009 gas price collapse and then the 2015-16 oil crash left it with the wrong rock twice. He had to sell Haynesville acreage and redeploy into oil while carrying debt that the 2016 market would not refinance cheaply.
turn: The 2011 decision to buy into the Delaware Basin ahead of the February 2012 IPO, which repriced the company from a gas driller to a Permian oil operator.

s: Cinemark Holdings DEF 14A filed 1 Apr 2026 citing Schedule 13G of 13 Aug 2025: Lee Roy Mitchell and affiliated entities 10,144,031 shares, 8.7 percent
m: 10,144,031 shares held with Button Tree Investments LLC and the Mitchell Special Trust II times the 36.60 dollar CNK close of 21 Aug 2026 = 371 million dollars; counts the disclosed Cinemark position only
did: Founded Cinemark in 1984 and built it to roughly 500 theatres and 5,800 screens, deliberately siting multiplexes in small and mid-size American cities the national chains skipped, then taking the same format to Brazil, Chile and Argentina from 1993.
why: Screen economics are set by rent and construction cost per seat, not by ticket price. Building in secondary US markets and then in Latin America gave Cinemark the lowest occupancy cost per screen of any major circuit, which is why it stayed solvent through two industry-wide bankruptcies that took its rivals.
obst: The 2000-2002 exhibition bust put Loews, United Artists, Carmike, General Cinema and Regal into Chapter 11 as overbuilt stadium-seating megaplexes cannibalised older screens; Cinemark was the only large US chain to come through without a bankruptcy filing, and repeated that in 2020-2022 when Cineworld's Regal failed.
turn: The 1993 entry into Chile, the start of a Latin American circuit that by 2019 was roughly 200 theatres and a currency-diversified profit stream no US rival had.

s: Green Brick Partners DEF 14A filed 22 May 2026, beneficial ownership as of 11 May 2026: 1,952,861 shares, 4.5 percent
m: 1,952,861 shares (including 300,000 in the Jim and Susan Brickman Grandchildrens Trust) times the 71.92 dollar GRBK close of 21 Aug 2026 = 140 million dollars
did: Formed JBGL Capital in 2008 with money from David Einhorn's Greenlight Capital and spent the crash buying distressed Dallas and Atlanta lots, then reverse-merged JBGL into the failed ethanol shell BioFuel Energy in October 2014 to create Nasdaq-listed Green Brick Partners.
why: Green Brick is a land developer that owns its builders, not a builder that rents land. It self-develops finished lots in infill Dallas and Atlanta locations and holds controlling equity in the builders that consume them, so it books both margins on the same dirt and never bids for lots at the top of a cycle.
obst: From 2008 to 2011 he had to keep persuading Einhorn to fund lot purchases while Dallas land values were still falling and no public market would touch a private lot bank; JBGL had no listed currency at all until the 2014 shell merger.
turn: The October 2014 reverse merger into BioFuel Energy Corp, which converted a Greenlight-funded private land partnership into a public homebuilder with access to equity and bond markets.

s: FirstCash Holdings DEF 14A filed 28 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership as of 13 Apr 2026: 822,797 shares, 1.88 percent; age 67 printed in the director table
m: 822,797 shares times the 225.28 dollar FCFS close of 21 Aug 2026 = 185 million dollars
did: Joined a small Texas pawn chain as CFO in 1992 after nine years at Price Waterhouse, became president in 1998 and CEO in 2006, and built FirstCash into roughly 3,000 pawn stores across the US and Latin America, merging with Cash America in 2016 and buying lease-to-own lender American First Finance in 2021.
why: Pawn is fully collateralised consumer credit with no charge-off risk and a licensing moat that keeps fintech out. Wessel pushed into Mexico from 1999, where store-level returns ran roughly double the US and sites beside Walmart de Mexico were still open, so Latin America came to supply over half the store base.
obst: The CFPB sued FirstCash in November 2021 for making pawn loans to active-duty servicemembers above the Military Lending Act rate cap; the company paid a 9 million dollar settlement in 2023 and had to rebuild its compliance stack at the same time as integrating the 1.17 billion dollar AFF acquisition.
turn: The September 2016 merger with Cash America International, which removed his only US scale competitor and made FirstCash the largest publicly traded pawn operator in the world.

s: D.R. Horton DEF 14A filed 10 Dec 2025, beneficial ownership as of 1 Dec 2025: 945,846 shares; age 69 printed in the director nominee table
m: 945,846 DHI shares times the 148.35 dollar close of 21 Aug 2026 = 140 million dollars; excludes his 25,000 Forestar shares and deferred compensation
did: Joined D.R. Horton as a division president in 1988, ran the Southeast region from 2005, became COO in 2013 and CEO from 2014 to 2023, taking revenue from about 8 billion to about 36 billion dollars and holding the number one US homebuilder position by closings; Executive Chairman since May 2024.
why: He converted D.R. Horton from a land owner into a land-light buyer of finished lots, using options and third-party developers plus its majority-owned Forestar, so inventory risk sat off the balance sheet and returns came from turns rather than land appreciation. That is what let it keep gaining share in a downturn.
obst: He took the CEO seat in 2014 and immediately argued for Express Homes, a stripped entry-level brand that deliberately cut average selling price and reported gross margin at a company whose investors were being sold a move-up recovery story.
turn: The 2014 launch of Express Homes, which went from zero to roughly a third of D.R. Horton closings within four years and locked up the only structurally undersupplied price band.

s: Encore Wire DEFM14A filed 22 May 2024 for the Prysmian merger: 863,511 shares, 5.36 percent, cashed out at 290.00 dollars per share; age 60 printed in the March 2024 DEF 14A
m: 863,511 shares times 290.00 dollars cash = 250 million dollars gross in the 2024 close, roughly 190 million after federal capital gains and NIIT with no Texas income tax
did: Joined Encore Wire in November 1989, the year it was founded in McKinney, as director of sales; became president in 1998, CEO in 2006 and chairman in 2014, and sold the company to Prysmian in 2024 for 4.2 billion dollars, 290 dollars a share in cash.
why: One campus. Copper rod, extrusion, warehouse and truck docks all sat on a single McKinney site, so Encore could quote and ship a complete building-wire order in days where rivals needed weeks from several plants. Distributors paid for that fill rate and the single site kept cost per pound lowest in the industry.
obst: Copper is the input and Encore refused to hedge it, so the 2008 and 2015 price collapses wrote down inventory and earnings while hedged rivals looked steadier; Jones held the no-hedging policy through shareholder pressure because it let Encore undercut those same rivals on the way down.
turn: The 2019-2023 expansion of the McKinney campus, roughly 300 million dollars of new plant finished just as data-centre and reshoring construction sent building-wire spreads to records and drew Prysmian's bid.

s: CBRE Group DEF 14A filed 3 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership as of 23 Mar 2026: 1,015,052 shares held directly; age 69 printed in the director table
m: 1,015,052 shares times the 152.10 dollar CBRE close of 21 Aug 2026 = 154 million dollars; excludes 50,731 shares in the Sulentic Family Foundation in which he has no pecuniary interest
did: Rose through Trammell Crow Company to CFO, CEO and chairman, sold it to CBRE in December 2006 for 2.2 billion dollars, ran CBRE's development, EMEA and Asia Pacific businesses, became CBRE chief executive in December 2012 and chairman in 2023, and moved the firm's global headquarters from Los Angeles to Dallas in 2020.
why: Brokerage revenue dies in a downturn, so he bought contracted work instead: Johnson Controls facilities in 2015 and Turner and Townsend in 2021 turned CBRE into a facilities and project management firm with roughly half its revenue under multi-year contract, which is why earnings stopped tracking the deal cycle.
obst: He inherited a balance sheet still carrying the debt from the top-of-cycle Trammell Crow purchase, and then in 2020 transactional revenue went to zero overnight while the market decided office space was structurally impaired, hitting both the brokerage and the investment-management books at once.
turn: The 2015 purchase of Johnson Controls' Global Workplace Solutions for 1.475 billion dollars, which tripled outsourcing revenue and made contracted facilities work CBRE's largest segment.

s: Signify Health DEFM14A filed 30 Sep 2022 for the CVS merger, interests of directors and officers tables; age 37 printed in the April 2022 DEF 14A director table
m: Merger consideration at 30.50 dollars per share: 182.7 million dollars for vested and unvested Aggregator units, 0.68 million for Class A shares, 10.3 million rollover options and 2.1 million rollover RSUs; roughly 196 million gross, about 140 million after tax
did: Left athenahealth to run Dallas-based Signify Health in April 2018, built its in-home health evaluation network to about two million Medicare Advantage member visits a year, took it public in February 2021 and sold it to CVS Health in March 2023 for 30.50 dollars a share, roughly 8 billion dollars.
why: Medicare Advantage plans are paid by CMS on documented risk scores, and the documentation has to happen in the member home. Signify owned the only national clinician network able to get inside those homes at scale, making it the toll gate to revenue plans could not otherwise capture, and a decade of hiring built it.
obst: Signify listed at 24 dollars in February 2021 and lost most of its value in 2022 when CMS ended the BPCI-A bundled-payment programme that its Episodes of Care segment depended on and simultaneously proposed limiting in-home diagnoses in risk adjustment, attacking both halves of the company at once.
turn: The mid-2022 decision to shut the Episodes of Care business and run a sale process, which produced a three-way auction and CVS's 30.50 dollar all-cash bid.

s: Forbes, 22 Nov 2021: 315 million dollars, her stake at the 2 billion dollar valuation set by SoftBank Vision Fund's 300 million dollar investment; her age given as 34 in the same piece
m: Forbes stake-times-valuation figure of 315 million, marked down about 10 percent for the compression in 2021-vintage private growth valuations since; no newer round has been disclosed
did: A Dallas personal shopper and fashion blogger, she and Baxter Box built rewardStyle in 2011 to pay bloggers commission when readers bought through their links, launched LIKEtoKNOW.it in 2014 so a screenshot of an Instagram photo returned shoppable links, and rebranded the whole thing LTK in 2021.
why: She solved attribution, not content. rewardStyle sat between dozens of retailer affiliate feeds and the creators, took a cut from both sides and kept the purchase data, so brands had to come through LTK to learn which creators actually sold. Instagram banning outbound links made her screenshot hack the only route.
obst: For the first years retailers would not pay commission on blogger traffic at all and she signed them one contract at a time; then from 2021 Instagram and TikTok shipped native affiliate and checkout tools aimed straight at LTK's reason to exist, forcing a rebuild from link plumbing into a standalone shopping app.
turn: The 2014 launch of LIKEtoKNOW.it, which turned an email-receipt hack around Instagram's no-links policy into a consumer product with millions of users.
